💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Champions League's league phase enters its back half this week, but already you could be forgiven for looking further ahead.
  • Sources indicate that wednesday will bring a few of the big teams on the top-24 bubble to consider -- Atletico Madrid and Manchester United in particular have their feet a little closer to the fire than ideal -- but before then, let's keep our eyes fixed on the top of the table.
  • Every match streams live on Paramount+, your home for every Champions League game all season long, plus replays, highlights and studio coverage breaking down the race for the top eight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Champions League's league phase enters its back half this week, but already you could be forgiven for looking further ahead. It is not so much that January will not provide some dramatic twists and turns, more that most of the contenders seem to have their affairs in order already. Yes, Bayern Munich have some work to do getting into the top eight, but most of the other sides from the top tier are in, well, the top tier.

Sources indicate that wednesday will bring a few of the big teams on the top-24 bubble to consider -- Atletico Madrid and Manchester United in particular have their feet a little closer to the fire than ideal -- but before then, let's keep our eyes fixed on the top of the table. Back-to-back winners Paris Saint-Germain look to be in a better state in table terms than they usually are, but might trouble be awaiting both them and Bayern?

Every match streams live on Paramount+, your home for every Champions League game all season long, plus replays, highlights and studio coverage breaking down the race for the top eight. If you haven't signed up yet, now's the time.

Recent weeks have not been kind to at least two of the three leading contenders. We'll come to Arsenal's injury issues shortly -- crucially, they appear to be less severe than had initially been feared -- but these have been brutal weeks for Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain.

Recent findings suggest that for the former, the headline news was the loss of Harry Kane until what he termed "the business end of the season," but that is only the start. Michael Olise is out of the game against Lille, having already been sidelined against Arsenal. Luis Diaz has played only nine times in the Bundesliga and Champions League. As for Jamal Musiala, well, things generally aren't going well when players' union FIFPRO is having words. There are few quality alternates in Vincent Kompany's squad. As Chuck Booth noted over the weekend, depth challenges have held Bayern back in Champions Leagues gone by. Rarely have those issues been so pronounced so early in the season.

Industry observers note that PSG do not want for quality backup, particularly in their front line. It is just that they would not have planned on leaning as heavily on it as they will have to now that Desire Doue has followed Khvicha Kvaratskhelia in suffering a major knee injury. Now, it is worth saying that Ousmane Dembele flanked by two of Ferran Torres, Maghnes Akliouche and Mika Godts could be very effective. However, for the time being at least, the benefit that Luis Enrique gets from his wholesale rotation in Ligue 1 is going to be, at best, significantly less pronounced. There are doubtless some prospects in the PSG academy who can take on extra minutes, but the value of Akliouche, Godts et al. eating domestic minutes drops when they also need to rock up in the games that count in the Champions League.

Now, of course, neither of these teams need to fear the worst. PSG top the league phase, and Bayern still have some gimme games (Slavia Prague, Manchester United) to get back up the standings. In the old group stage, perhaps Bayern would have paid the price for their early-season injuries. Instead, where the Champions League is concerned, they need only to focus on getting their guys back for February. No such prospects for PSG, but they still have those midfielders and those defenders. Your heart hardly bleeds.

If you are the field, though, this might be a year where a path opens up. The coming days might hint at who can claim it. Real Madrid have selection dilemmas of their own, but have won nine straight in La Liga and the Champions League. Yan Diomande and Arda Guler flanking Kylian Mbappe works exceptionally well. Those wingers make for a slightly more effective defensive unit, but wins over Roma and AEK Athens have pointed to a glass jaw that better teams might shatter. There is a similar question over Barcelona, whose ferocious pressing shatters lesser opponents but teeters dangerously when their passes per defensive action drift into double figures.

In a recent development, liverpool? They may not have the engine room to control knockout ties. The most intriguing dark horse, at least for this week, might be Manchester City. Then again, aren't they always the most intriguing team right now? Certainly, in their domestic games, they are playing like a team expecting the worst from the Premier League disciplinary procedure, intent on taking itself out of the title race before the probable points deduction does it anyway. Their 1-1 draw with Fulham betrayed a team that has the quality to win but not the intensity.

Sources indicate that is that a tap you can switch on and off? After all, even if they are sent to the Championship or beyond, they could still embarrass England's footballing authority by qualifying for the Champions League as holders. Even at 85% capacity so far this season, they profile in the inner circle across Europe's top five leagues. There is a path for a team that wants to get it together. Is that City?

Industry observers note that when David Raya made his way off the field clutching his left arm, anguish stretched across his face, you could be forgiven for thinking that that season was happening to Arsenal again. They have recruited high-quality backups in almost every position and probably would have a higher-grade reserve goalkeeper if it weren't such a hard sell to cover for the best in the world in his position. And so when Kepa Arrizabalaga entered the fray, hearts sank in the away end at St. James' Park.

They soared on Monday afternoon when Mikel Arteta confirmed that Raya would not need surgery and that initial tests "revealed something much more encouraging" given the enormous pain the Spaniard seemed to be in. The No. 1 will be unavailable against Borussia Dortmund, but he has not been ruled out of Sunday's clash with Manchester City. It was against that opponent that Kepa's reputation was so soured, a horror show in the EFL Cup final in which he conceded both of the shots on target he faced.

Since then, he has started only three games: elimination by Southampton in the FA Cup, where he was just as bad, a dead rubber against Crystal Palace and an EFL Cup win at Ipswich. Though it was the goals he conceded that cost Arsenal at Wembley, his distribution came under just as intense a spotlight, his inability to navigate the Man City press stalling attacks at their starting point. Raya is a master of breaking teams with his passing. Since the start of the season, he leads all Premier League goalkeepers in line-breaking passes under pressure and in passes that break through three lines. Asking your backup to replicate Raya's range is borderline unreasonable. If a goalkeeper could pass that well, they wouldn't be warming the Arsenal bench.

Anyway, the primary job of a goalkeeper, even in 2026, is actually to keep the ball out of the net. And while Kepa hasn't done great at that lately, it is hardly like he has been playing in rhythm. When he is, the 32-year-old is absolutely fine. Good enough, in fact, that when Arsenal signed him in the summer of 2025, it was viewed as something of a coup. In his year with Bournemouth, Kepa had profiled as an above-average shot-stopper at volume, saving 71.3% of efforts he faced and conceding two fewer goals than the expected goals value of the shots he faced. It was the same in Kepa's final year as a regular starter with Chelsea, where he kept nine clean sheets in 29 games. There are weaknesses in Kepa's game beyond his passing. He does not particularly command his area when crosses come in, certainly not compared to Raya. He hardly flies off his line like his compatriot either, but it is worth reaffirming that the standard he is being held against is the man voted the best goalkeeper in the world by his fellow professionals. Kepa is not going to raise a team's ceiling like the man he will likely replace on Wednesday -- what a wasted endeavor this would be if Illan Meslier starts -- but put him behind the best shot-suppressing defense in the business over an extended period and he would probably be good enough to ensure that Arsenal's ambitions are not capped. It would appear, however, that we will not get a definitive answer on that for a while yet. That is no bad thing for Arteta and Arsenal.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nwaneri returns to his parent club tonight in the Champions League with the Bundesliga giants and is eligible to face Arsenal despite still being owned by the Gunners.
  • But beyond this campaign, his future remains uncertain, with manager Mikel Arteta even recently alluding to the teenager's struggles at Signal Iduna Park.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ethan Nwaneri's Arsenal career appears to be floundering, with the on-loan Borussia Dortmund teenager facing a further transfer setback.

Nwaneri returns to his parent club tonight in the Champions League with the Bundesliga giants and is eligible to face Arsenal despite still being owned by the Gunners.

But beyond this campaign, his future remains uncertain, with manager Mikel Arteta even recently alluding to the teenager's struggles at Signal Iduna Park.

Nwaneri became the Premier League's youngest-ever player in 2022 at the age of 15 – with Max Dowman later taking that record – before establishing himself in the 2024/25 season as a serious option on the right wing for the Gunners.

But after going out on loan at Marseille last term and heading to Dortmund this time, the teenager is yet to impress, with Arteta even admitting this week that “moments are not enough” for Nwaneri in his development and that consistency must follow.

A report from Sport Witness, likewise, reads as bad news for the 19-year-old, with the Gunners now pursuing a move for Gilberto Mora as soon as January.

Mora was the youngest player selected for the 2026 World Cup and has impressed hugely in his native Mexico, courting the attention of virtually every major club in Europe.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In attacking midfield areas, Arsenal already have the likes of Martin Odegaard, Mikel Merino, Eberechi Eze and Max Dowman – with the latter two options on the wing – and should Arsenal bring in another teenage talent, Nwaneri's first-team opportunities would appear even scarcer.

FourFourTwo understands that the Gunners were open to offers for the starlet over the summer, opting to retain him and develop him at one of the best finishing schools in European football, though the paths of Nwaneri and Hale End colleague Myles Lewis-Skelly have been drastically different, thanks, in part, due to competition for places.

With Liverpool also circling for Mora, however, the Gunners may well have to present a particularly enticing package to secure the 18-year-old.

According to the report, the youngster has a release clause of around €25 million, making any move for him particularly costly – and suggesting that the Gunners could well incorporate him into their first team immediately.

Nwaneri, meanwhile, is valued by Transfermarkt at €25m. Arsenal return to Champions League action tonight against Dortmund at the Emirates Stadium.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By MICHAEL PAVITT, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 09:18 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 09:19 EST, 27 November 2026.

Bolivian referee Jordy Aleman was stunningly seen appearing to punch a player after being surrounded in the aftermath of the Bolivian Cup final.

Footage highlighted Aleman being surrounded by Real Potosi players following the final whistle of the match, the second leg of the final.

Real Potosi had proved unable to overturn a 3-1 first leg deficit against Always Ready in their home leg as they were held to a goalless draw.

Real Potosi had finished the match down to 10 men after Kevin Villegas was sent off in stoppage time for violent conduct.

Players had surrounded Aleman following the final whistle to contest refereeing decisions during the match, with the official then appearing to strike out at Real Potosi goalkeeper Christian Martinez.

According to Marca, the referee then highlighted a further four red cards to players and dismissed a further three members of Real Potosi's coaching staff.

Bolivian referee Jordy Aleman was surrounded by Real Potosi players after the Bolivian Cup final. Source: ESPN.

In a recent development, footage highlighted Aleman lashing out at Real Potosi goalkeeper Christian Martinez amid the confrontation. Source: ESPN.

It has been revealed that martinez later admitted to insulting the referee, who was surrounded by security after the incident. Source: ESPN.

Footage then demonstrated Aleman surrounded by security in the aftermath of the incident.

Martinez later revealed that he had told the official to 'go to hell' and that he 'hoped his mother dies', leading to the referee striking out at him.

The Argentine goalkeeper remarked he had been left with a bloodied mouth following the punch.

Martinez later issued a statement on social media to confirm he will not pursue legal action or make a complaint about the official following the extraordinary incident.

'After what happened at the end of the second leg of the Paceña Cup final against Always Ready, where I was punched by referee Jordy Alemán Peralta, I have decided not to initiate legal action or file complaints with the sports authorities,' Martinez wrote on social media.

'My intention is to put this episode behind me and prevent this situation from continuing to generate conflicts, while remaining fully available to the competent authorities for any clarification that may be necessary.

'Nothing should overshadow the extraordinary season we've had,.

'We competed until the very last minute and gave everything on the field for this jersey.'.

The Bolivian Football Federation are yet to confirm the sanction Aleman will receive following the incident.

The organisation's disciplinary rules give them the power to impose a ban of up to three years, as well as a fine equivalent to 20 times the national minimum wage.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that with the MLS Cup playoffs now in full swing, it also means that we are beginning to see who is taking home honors at the end of the season. Nashville SC have already seen Maxwell Woledzi win Defender of the Year and Bran Shwake earn Goalkeeper of the Year honors, and they have potential honorees up and down the awards docket alongside the youngest MVP finalist in league history, Cavan Sullivan, who has taken home young player of the year honors. Antoine Griezmann has also won Newcomer of the Year in only half of a season with Orlando City SC.

Check out the winners and finalists so far:.

Leading Nashville SC to a record low of 25 goals conceded and tying Tony Meola's record for the most clean sheets in an MLS season with 16, Brian Schwake has taken home Goalkeeper of the Year honors by a landslide, beating out finalists Matt Turner and Roman Bürki. In only his first season as the full-time starter for Nashville, Schwake took the reins and didn't look back, also debuting for the U.S. Men's National Team due to his success. He also set club records for wins, penalty kick saves (three), save percentage (78.4%), and goals against average (0.76).

In a recent development, it's astounding that Eduard Lowen is playing soccer, considering what the few years have looked like for him. In March of this year, his wife Ilona died from brain cancer after they managed through her diagnosis, with Lowen taking time off from the game to support her and her family. He returned to MLS play in April, scoring in his first start of the season for St. Louis City SC, but then was traded to San Jose after the World Cup break. During that time with San Jose, he became an important part of their playoff run with one goal and three assists.

Becoming the youngest MVP finalist in league history at only 17, it should come as no surprise that Cavan Sullivan has won Young Player of the Year, beating out the Red Bull Fresh York duo of Julian Hall and Adri Mehmeti. During the World Cup break, Sullivan spent time training with the Union's MLS Next Pro side instead of taking the time off for himself, and the results demonstrated in the second half of the season as he helped lead the Union into a playoff spot. With nine goals and 14 assists (including secondary assists), no teenager has ever been involved in more goals in a season than Sullivan, and it has also led to his first cap with the United States men's national team, where he was able to grab his first goal against Mexico. If this is the tip of the iceberg, we're in for something special, considering that this has been a banner year for young players in MLS, with more minutes being given to teenagers than ever before. The future is in good hands as the kids are leveling up each day.

With Guilherme receiving MVP votes to become a finalist for the award, it was going to take a special performance for someone else to win Newcomer of the Year, and joining Orlando City SC, Antoine Griezmann did just that. Prior to his arrival, this was a team floundering below the playoff line after moving on from manager Oscar Pareja. In only a half-season, he came in and scored 14 goals and assisted eight more as the first player ever to produce 20 goal contributions in only half a season, while turning this team into contenders. It's going to be tough in the playoffs for Griezmann to overcome the defense, but considering what he has already done with the squad, there's no reason why Orlando should be counted out with the Frenchman next to Justin Ellis.

According to recent reports, en route to setting a points record with 77 points to win the Supporters' Shield, Nashville SC were also led by a record-setting defense that only let the ball into the back of the net 25 times in an entire campaign. That success was rewarded with all three finalists for Defender of the Year coming from Nashville, but it's their newest signing that took home the award. Joining from Norwegian club Fredrikstad ahead of the season, Woledzi didn't need much time to adjust, appearing in every regular-season match and helping Nashville build from the back to maintain possession. It was a team effort to tie the MLS clean sheet record with 17 during the season, so it's only natural for one of their defenders to get the honors this season.

But just how special is Tresoldi, and which European giants could be in the running to sign him in 2027?

Nicolò Tresoldi silences the San Siro 🤫Club Brugge stun Inter 🥶 pic.twitter.com/D8TIEn6b9C.

It has been revealed that tresoldi was born in Cagliari, Sardinia, in 2004, during the summer months when his family would regularly spend time on the island. His connection to Sardinia stemmed from his maternal grandfather, who worked there as a golf instructor. Thanks to this family connection, they had a house on the island and would spend part of their summers there, but because of his mother's job, he moved with his family to Hannover in 2017, when he was 13.

Tresoldi, who until then had played tennis more regularly, decided to start his soccer career in the Hannover academy, where he debuted with the second team before making his first-team debut in 2022. He immediately drew interest from multiple European clubs, and in the summer of 2025 he joined Club Brugge in Belgium, his first major move as a professional soccer player. In his first season at the club, he scored 23 goals in 58 games, including four in the Champions League's league phase, and he has started his second season even better, with 15 goals in all competitions so far, including that unforgettable hat-trick against Inter in Milan.

It has been revealed that next year will also be the year he makes a final decision about which national team he wants to represent. Tresoldi is eligible for Germany, Italy and Argentina. In 2023, he decided to join the German U21 team, and he now intends to see out the entire cycle through the 2027 U21 European Championship, which will take place in the summer. Until then, he won't make a final decision, but both Italy coach Roberto Mancini and Germany coach Jürgen Klopp have expressed interest in calling him up.

Speaking on the topic and about Tresoldi's future, Klopp mentioned: "It doesn't mean that he has made a decision against Germany or Italy. We don't want to put any pressure on the players. It's a sensitive matter, and we will respect whatever decision he makes, without rushing him." Mancini, on the other hand, seemed more optimistic about him choosing Italy: "I've spoken to Tresoldi myself. He needs to feel that he wants to represent our national team. Given that he was born in Italy and has an Italian father, I believe there is a possibility. We hope he makes the right choice; he knows how much he would mean to us." Argentina can also hope to call him up, as his mother is from there, and he could be included in Lionel Scaloni's squad. However, Italy and Germany are his most likely choices.

Before that, he will also be the subject of transfer rumors starting in the early months of the new year, as many top European clubs are looking for a new striker. AC Milan have to be on that list, as the Rossoneri will likely sign a new striker to play alongside Gonçalo Ramos, even though Club Brugge reportedly value him at around $50 million. At the same time, we need to monitor what Bayern Munich do in the January transfer window, as Harry Kane's injury might force the German side to change strategy in the short term. For sure, 2027 will be the year of Tresoldi, as he now focuses his attention on two moves that will shape his future.

Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.
  • Recent findings suggest that "This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation.
  • In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.

Recent findings suggest that "This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods.".

In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.

"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar noted, referring to the effects of climate change.

"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.

Climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.

Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.

As it deals with the effects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.

According to recent reports, in the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.

Industry observers note that while using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.

"Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar stated. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, at the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.

Industry observers note that environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.

The Climate Accountability Institute said it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.

Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.

"That has been also a sticky problem. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way.".

The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.

In a recent development, "You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar mentioned, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming.".

Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.

Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar said, describing them as a potential "breakthrough.".

In a recent development, carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.

"Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar mentioned.

Carbon credits have been promoted as an vital source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.

"We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar stated, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.

"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed.".

The Liverpool fans did not miss a beat. They never do. “Poch is at the wheel,” they goaded as this calamity unfolded. But at the wheel of what, a clown car? The look of thunder on Mauricio Pochettino’s face stated it all as he got off to the worst start of any Manchester United manager – or head coach – in 100 years.

In a recent development, the Pochettino bandwagon rolled into town with the usual fanfare of a new era, new belief, new hope; and then the wheels came off, the doors collapsed and the engine exploded. The opening quarter of an hour really was that farcical.

In that time, away to Liverpool of all places, they were 2-0 down, a player down – and down and out. If Pochettino had any uncertainty over the scale of the task ahead of him, there it was laid bare. Of course United had some mitigation. They played almost the entire game with 10 men, but teams have coped with that before and shown far more resistance and resilience. By the time United did that, it was game over. No one expected a quick fix, but come on.

In a recent development, any regrets, Mauricio? Whatever the salary, he could be forgiven for having a few as he watched on. This is a far cry from being in charge of the United States and watching them roll over Haiti 8-0 on aggregate, as he did last week. If Liverpool had been more ruthless, it could have been 8-0 here.

In the end it was 4-0 – the same scoreline by which Lal Hilditch lost his first game at United, away to Bolton Wanderers in October 1926. Hilditch was a stop-gap player-manager and former central defender Pochettino may well have been tempted to bring himself on, even at the age of 54. He could barely have done worse.

It has been revealed that pochettino, too, can take some responsibility. Eyebrows were certainly raised when he dropped Harry Maguire – who he then had to bring on after 22 minutes – to hand Matthijs de Ligt his first Premier League start in 357 days. De Ligt was then at fault for the first and, arguably, the second goal.

Did the head coach start with a back three or a back four? The players seemed confused. It eventually ended up as a back five.

According to recent reports, but this was a collective failing for United. From the top – with director of football Jason Wilcox caught on camera with his head buried in his coat – through the club and out on the pitch. Pochettino is substantial on building a culture. So he has to abolish the comedy and the chaos and restore credibility.

United are deep in a relegation battle. Have no doubt. Eight points after 11 games means they are presently on target for fewer than 28 points, which is a lower points-per-game total than when they were relegated in 1974.

Recent findings suggest that the work needed at United is monumental. The transfer strategy has been inexplicable, with the decision being to rebuild the attack last year, the midfield this summer and wait until next year to remodel the defence. The folly of that has been exposed by the fact that United have conceded 34 goals already this season, the most in the top five European leagues.

Bruno Fernandes says he has shelved talks over a latest contract because it is not the “right moment” for discussions over his future as Manchester United captain.

Fernandes, 32, is out of contract next summer although United have a 12-month option to extend his deal to 2028.

The Portugal midfielder is understood to have rejected two contract offers from United since the summer but said all his focus needs to be on trying to help the team out of their current plight.

United head into Sunday’s game against Liverpool at Anfield second from bottom in the Premier League.

“We spoke about the contract at the end of last season,” Fernandes told Sky Sports.

“We came in at the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but about the context of the team and the club, I just put that to a side because I don’t think it’s the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations.

“The most vital thing now is that the club gets back to winning games.”.

Fernandes said claims he wants more money or a longer-term deal on offer are incorrect and that if finances were the issue he would have left Old Trafford before now. The captain has previously rejected lucrative offers from Saudi Arabia.

“The club offered me a latest contract, so I think that, from their side, reveals that they want me to stay,” he said.

It has been revealed that “There’s no negotiations ongoing, but I’ve seen people saying that ‘He’s asked for more money, he’s asked for more years’. If I wanted more money, I wouldn’t be here.

Recent findings suggest that “I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United. I could have been in a place that is much warmer than Manchester.

“Two summers ago, three summers ago, last summer, I always had the chance to leave and I always chose to be here.

“The thing is, I’ve always revealed how much I care about the club and how much I want to win at this club. And I always stated, in the moment the club thinks it’s time for me to move on, I will move on.

Sources indicate that “I’m not going to be the player that I’ve seen many in this time at Manchester United. They’re going to stay here just by staying, just finish my contract and then we will see. In the moment the club says, ‘Bruno, it’s time to part ways’, I’m going to be the first one walking out the door.”.

United chief executive Omar Berrada noted of Fernandes on Friday that it was “true that we’re having conversations about his newly introduced contract” but that the club preferred “to keep that private”.

Having been voted PFA Player of the Year last season, Fernandes’ form has dropped off this term like that of the team.

He was dropped for the 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth in the wake of a 4-1 drubbing by Como when he criticised the tactics and approach of then head coach Michael Carrick.

Mauricio Pochettino, Carrick’s successor, confirmed on Friday that Fernandes would remain as captain.

Fernandes said the United fans had been “far too patient with us” and hopes Pochettino - who wanted to bring the Portuguese to Spurs in 2019 - will bring a fresh energy.

“He’s someone that likes to bring a very good energy to the team, someone very positive, very strong, strict, said it straight away that he won’t allow us to not give him what he demands from the team, from each player,” Fernandes said.

“He wants the club to succeed so much, he wants to win games, and that’s pretty clear and obvious by the way he and his staff speak and want us to improve.

It has been revealed that “Obviously [in 2019] I was a very young player that was eager to come to the Premier League. They had [Harry] Kane there, they had Dele Alli, Son, the chance of playing with those players in front was very attractive.”.

According to recent reports, pochettino arrived in the country on Wednesday after his final matches in charge of the US national team. He has inherited a squad with some players who have publicly criticised their own coach and technical director this season during their slide down the table.

The new United head coach, who has a contract until 2029, mentioned “culture” seven times in his first club interview in a pointed analysis of the work he needs to do at Old Trafford, starting with this weekend’s match against Liverpool at Anfield.

“The culture, to create the culture is the most vital,” Pochettino stated. “To have the culture is the most important. Create the habit, the principle and I think that is what we want to create. We need to look forward and to find a way to create the best habit and the culture that makes us to be close to win every single game.”.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the game everyone has been waiting for as Manchester United prepare to face Liverpool at Anfield in Mauricio Pochettino’s first outing in charge of the club.

Quiet international break at Man Utd? Don’t be ridiculous. Following a dismal start to the season, which has left today’s visitors 19th in the league table with just one win from 10 matches, Michael Carrick was eventually relieved of his duties as head coach and replaced by Pochettino, who left his role as the United States head coach after two years at the helm.

Pochettino has been handed the unenviable task of attempting to rescue Man Utd’s desperate situation in an extremely tumultuous time for the club under the co-ownership of the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe.

Recent findings suggest that “I think what we need to do is to be very open-minded and try to do our best to try to perform and the players need to buy the idea of we need to improve, and that is our job. After a few days working, the job is to try to find a way to, from Sunday, perform and to start getting the results that the club historically needs, and it’s because Manchester United needs to be in a place, in a different place than we are now.”.

Why Arsenal’s crazy festive fixture run could hand them the Premier League title in record time

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Between now and then, Arsenal’s longest away day takes them just 22 kilometres to Brentford - Google Maps says the average person could walk from the Emirates to the Gtech in under four hours, never mind a professional footballer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Having made their longest Premier League away trip of the season to Newcastle last week, Arsenal can settle into familiar surroundings for the festive period: the Gunners don’t leave London again until mid-January when they travel to Hull.

Between now and then, Arsenal’s longest away day takes them just 22 kilometres to Brentford - Google Maps says the average person could walk from the Emirates to the Gtech in under four hours, never mind a professional footballer.

That’s the third of 11 straight games in the capital for the Gunners, which will become 12 if they’re drawn at home in the third round of the FA Cup, beginning with Tuesday’s Champions League clash against Borussia Dortmund. Recent history suggests an interesting theory about such home comforts.

Industry observers note that eleven games into their title defence, Arsenal sit second in the Premier League away table with four wins, one draw and one defeat from six games on the road. Not that it’s anything fresh for the Gunners to occupy such heights: they’ve boasted the top flight’s best away record in each of the last four seasons.

Industry observers note that and that comes with the territory of being a London club. Across the last 10 Premier League campaigns not impacted by pandemic crowd restrictions (so excluding 2019/20 and 2020/21), only once have more clubs from London had a bottom-half away record than a top-half away record. That was last term, when four of the seven London clubs finished in the bottom 10 of the away table (Crystal Palace, Brentford, Fulham and West Ham).

In each of the other nine seasons in question, at least 57 per cent of the Premier League’s London clubs have finished with one of the best 10 away records in the division; in 2016/17, all five of them did (Chelsea, Tottenham, Arsenal, Palace and West Ham).

So, is it an advantage to be a London club?

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

There’s not really a simple answer to that question (sorry), but we can still pull together some interesting takeaways.

It has been revealed that this season, the average Premier League club will travel 153 kilometres for an away fixture. For two clubs, that average climbs to over 300km: the league’s two most north-easterly sides, Sunderland (350km) and Newcastle (347km), and the most south-westerly, Bournemouth (317km). Conversely, one side will travel a touch under 200km on average: Coventry (198km) – in that sense, you might consider the Sky Blues the ultimate Midlands club.

But the top-flight’s six London clubs all sit in the bottom eight of the league in terms of average away travel distance, with Palace travelling the furthest (227km) and Spurs the least far (202km). And the very fact that those sides account for just over a quarter of the division means short trips are a regular occurrence.

And for Arsenal, this 11-match stretch that sees them go no further than Brentford could not fall at a better time than the notoriously hectic festive period – certainly when it comes to maximising recovery time between fixtures, which come thick and fast an average of one game every 4.2 days between now and January 5 (though it’s worth noting that turnaround is still below the UEFA-recommended minimum window of five days between matches).

Recent findings suggest that could the timing of Arsenal’s London residency, so to speak, prove crucial to another successful Premier League title push? Well, they’re already six points clear at the top and look like they could walk it, given Manchester City’s dramatic recent drop-off, but minimising time spent on the road during one of the busiest stages of the campaign seems unlikely to work to their detriment.

In a recent development, that being mentioned, a quick word on Chelsea: the Blues have left London three times all season but are languishing in mid-table in the Premier League and are out of the Carabao Cup. So, maybe there’s something to be said for getting out of town on a more regular basis. Besides, it’s not like elite-level players these days are travelling in anything less than luxury, is it?

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

German mathematician Bernhard Riemann formulated his famous conjecture in 1859.Credit: Smithsonian Libraries and Archives (CC0).

On 20 November, mathematicians made two competing announcements about solving the Riemann hypothesis — perhaps the most notable open problem in mathematics.

It has been revealed that the question had remained unanswered since it was formulated in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann (1826–66). His statement is central to the theory of prime numbers, the whole numbers that cannot be evenly divided by any other number except themselves or 1.

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

The hypothesis concerns the distribution of primes, and it is crucial because these numbers are central to all of maths. “There is nothing more basic and more fundamental in mathematics that the prime numbers,” says Álvaro Lozano-Robledo, a mathematician at the University of Connecticut in Storrs.

Riemann arrived at his idea by studying prime numbers as waves — in a way that presages the way music recordings are compressed into mp3 files — and his hypothesis is usually described in abstruse-sounding language. But at its heart, the idea boils down to a statistical test that is familiar to any scientist who’s ever analysed data.

Nature breaks down the Riemann hypothesis.

Industry observers note that mathematicians want to know how predictable the prime numbers are. The German scientist Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855), who many consider to be the greatest mathematician in history, had noticed in the late eighteenth century (when he was a teenager) that if you pick any whole number, the odds that it’s a prime depend on the number’s size. Primes slowly become sparser as numbers become bigger. Gauss observed that their frequency seems to depend on (or, is inversely proportional to) the number of digits. Roughly speaking, among numbers with k digits, one in every k of them is a prime.

Sources indicate that in Riemann’s time, a half-century after Gauss’s guess, there was still no rigorous proof of this. In a landmark paper in 1859, Riemann stated his belief that the late Gauss, who had been one of his mentors at the University of Göttingen, had been right.

But Riemann — who was a “daring” thinker, notes maths historian Rossana Tazzioli at the University of Lille in France — went much further. He proposed that Gauss’s “one in every k” guess was a good statistical prediction, meaning that the frequency of the primes should not fluctuate away from it too much. In other words, Riemann made a guess about the margin of error of Gauss’s prediction.

Recent findings suggest that if true, this ‘Riemann hypothesis’ would make primes’ behaviour similar to that of a random process, such as a series of coin tosses. More precisely, he suggested that when you count the primes among the first n whole numbers, fluctuations would take a form that many scientists are familiar with: “The idea of the Riemann hypothesis is that the error term looks a lot like √n, which is what any random model will give you,” claims Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal in Canada.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis.

Such square-root terms pop up everywhere in data analysis, because they control the shrinking of a margin of error as the number n of data points grows.

Recent findings suggest that in his paper, Riemann did much more than guess. He introduced tools that would constitute the basis for much of the work on number theory — the branch of mathematics that concerns integers, primes and divisibility — in the following centuries.

First, by developing fresh techniques in analysis — another word for advanced calculus — as he went along, Riemann constructed the ‘Riemann ζ function’ (ζ is the Greek letter ‘zeta’).

In a recent development, riemann then revealed that the function embodied an enormous amount of information about prime numbers. First, he proved that the solutions to the equation ζ (z) = 0 — where z is a point on a plane — encode the statistical distribution of prime numbers along the number line. To do so, Riemann employed a type of Fourier analysis, the type of maths that nowadays enables the compression of music into compact mp3 files by breaking sound waves down into sinusoidal components.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that LONDON -- To lose one elegantly-earned lead, Mr.
  • The real impact of two points dropped tonight probably won't become clear until February and the draw for the last 16.
  • Industry observers note that of more immediate concern for Arteta, who was unstinting in his praise of Arsenal's "brilliant performance", is that this team's very good football is not enough to overwhelm their opposition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that LONDON -- To lose one elegantly-earned lead, Mr. Arteta, may be regarded as a misfortune; to lose two looks like carelessness. Three days after frittering away their lead at Newcastle, Arsenal repeated in the Champions League, as Borussia Dortmund became the first team to stop Mikel Arteta's side from winning a league phase game at the Emirates Stadium.

The real impact of two points dropped tonight probably won't become clear until February and the draw for the last 16. A year ago, topping the league table set Arsenal on a favorable path to the Champions League final. There are, of course, no guarantees that they would not get that as a lower seed but a repeat finish in the top two looks unlikely, with Real Madrid and Paris Saint-Germain both in possession of 100% records.

Industry observers note that of more immediate concern for Arteta, who was unstinting in his praise of Arsenal's "brilliant performance", is that this team's very good football is not enough to overwhelm their opposition. It is worth noting, at this early juncture, that this team did position itself to potentially overwhelm the German league leaders. As is so often the case with the Gunners, we're assessing them against standards that would be considered unreasonable for 99% of teams. Usually, when you put up 2.2 xG on Borussia Dortmund and give up 0.9, you can be as pleased with your side as Arteta was in public. In private, you can rest assured that he will be as detail-obsessed as this column in attempting to explain why such sustained spells of excellence still end in a share of the points.

As at St. James' Park on Saturday night, for 45 minutes here, Arsenal were delicious, a true smorgasbord of footballing delights. Piero Hincapie popping up as an additional center forward, Christos Tzolis gliding off the left, Declan Rice barnstorming from third center back to second attacking midfielder in the space of a single pressing trigger.

It has been revealed that borussia Dortmund arrived in north London tied with their hosts for the fewest goals conceded in Europe's top five leagues. Niko Kovac's back five, with three robust midfielders ahead of them, looked like it should be enough to stifle the Gunners. Instead, they were overwhelmed, pulled here and there in their attempts to track position-lite red shirts.

Arsenal's excellence got the goal it deserved, a larruping strike from Viktor Gyokeres that moved one way, then the other, with such extravagance you rather wondered if the Australian cricket team had given the ball a going over beforehand. Nico Schlotterbeck seemed convinced he'd got an edge on it. Gregor Kobel looked dumbfounded. Even Gyokeres' belated donning of the Bane mask suggested he thought there had been some external force aiding him. Not so. You just hit it that well, Viktor.

Recent findings suggest that from there, Arsenal had all they needed to wrap this game up in style. Their press constricted the game into the spaces where Martin Odegaard could excel. Noni Madueke was even more menacing, a player who seems to have unlocked himself in little over a month. They kept getting into the final third. They kept getting shots, too, 14 of them before the half was out. The problem was how bad those shots were. A baker's dozen and one spare and Arsenal couldn't put up a full expected goal before the break.

Recent findings suggest that too often, moves ended prematurely because someone in red fancied taking a swing from range. Eight of their first-half shots were from outside the box. Gyokeres tried a few heat checks; come the final whistle, he was as cold as the north London night. Declan Rice has evidently read Arteta saying that he should try more shots from range. The ones from outside the box, one of which really brought the oohs as it flew over the bar, weren't even his worst. Not squaring for Madueke in the first half or Gyokeres in the second really was a spurning of prime opportunities.

It has been revealed that if this rush to shoot from range were a one-off, you could frame it as Arteta did in his post-match press conference, "a variation in relation to the opponent, the situation that you have". And yet Arsenal have been trying from range more frequently this season, from fewer than four shots per game in 2025-26 to nearly five this term, a 23% increase in shot volume from range. Against Newcastle, the proportions were lower but twice in an excellent 45 minutes, they shot when they could have worked the ball into a better spot. Arteta has spoken about unlocking the long-range potential of his team. Those who know his thinking often frame his obsession with adding "gamechangers" to his roster in terms of players who can beat a man and strike one from deep.

They still take a lower proportion of efforts from outside the box than most teams in Europe's top five leagues but most teams in Europe's top five leagues don't employ Martin Odegaard. For now, the sample size and the variation might be so small as to be explained through happenstance or circumstances rather than design. Bukayo Saka's injury has removed one of Arsenal's primary penalty-box threats from this team. His replacement, Madueke, is still honing his shot profile, if we're being generous.

It has been revealed that there is also value to a team that faces so many low blocks proving themselves to be willing to strike from range. Fail to close down an Eberechi Eze and you might well be picking the ball out of your net soon after. Get those defenders moving out of position to close down the shot and an angle to a better opening might present itself.

It is a hard balance to strike. Tonight, Arsenal did not quite manage it: prime positions turned into subprime shots because trigger fingers got itchy.

According to recent reports, A driving run from Joane Gadou took him away from Christos Tzolis, as the midfield busied themselves with other matters. Maximilian Beier received the ball in the box and smartly turned away from Gabriel before drilling low past Kepa Arrizabalaga. Even a defense as excellent as Arsenal's can't keep your average Premier League or Champions League opponent from clicking once. The levels are just too high.

An upswing in pressure in the final 35 minutes brought enough moments to leave Arteta baffled. "There is an element of luck here because how in hell some of the goals they haven't gone in, I don't know. Some of the days last year we hit somebody and it was an own goal.

"Quality sometimes [is missing], or [there is a] rush, or [a need] to have a bit of composure, or to read the next pass a little bit better; the execution can be better, but everything that is in between that, I think was really, really good.".

Industry observers note that he is not wrong. It just seems even more careless to let two points slip away because they could not quell their shot-first instincts.

North Macedonia remains stalled on its EU path after 21 years as a candidate

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Union's enlargement drive has regained momentum: Montenegro could become the bloc's 28th member in 2028, while Albania is rapidly advancing through accession talks and could complete accession negotiations by the end of 2027 if it maintains its current pace of reforms.
  • But North Macedonia, an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession.
  • That contrast will be particularly evident at Wednesday's EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Union's enlargement drive has regained momentum: Montenegro could become the bloc's 28th member in 2028, while Albania is rapidly advancing through accession talks and could complete accession negotiations by the end of 2027 if it maintains its current pace of reforms.

But North Macedonia, an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession.

That contrast will be particularly evident at Wednesday's EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels.

"The Western Balkans' future is in the European Union. Their accession is our priority, our shared ambition and a crucial geopolitical investment in these turbulent times," European Council President Antonio Costa remarked ahead of the meeting.

North Macedonia formally opened accession talks with the EU in July 2022 but has yet to open the first of the EU's six negotiating clusters, the groups of policy areas through which candidates align their laws and institutions with EU standards.

But the lack of movement does not mean the country is unprepared for membership.

EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos noted in November that North Macedonia was "among the countries with the highest level of preparedness" in aligning with EU law and had recently accelerated reforms under the EU Growth Plan.

However, she added, "the handbrake on its accession negotiations is still on.".

Kos mentioned that to release this handbrake and open the first cluster, North Macedonia must adopt the constitutional amendment agreed with the EU in 2022.

For years, a dispute with Greece over the country's name blocked North Macedonia's progress along the EU accession path.

Although the 2018 Prespa Agreement resolved the dispute, and the country changed its constitutional name, clearing the way for NATO membership, a breakthrough on EU accession did not follow.

It has been revealed that bulgaria later blocked the process amid disputes over history, language and identity. A compromise brokered during the French EU presidency in 2022 lifted the veto but made further progress conditional on North Macedonia amending its constitution to explicitly include Bulgarians among the country's recognized communities.

The amendment requires a two-thirds majority in parliament, which has so far proved unattainable.

From the EU's perspective, this is no longer a Bulgarian veto, but a condition North Macedonia accepted as part of its negotiating framework.

In a recent development, "It [North Macedonia] is not blocked by a member state. It is blocked because it doesn't want to date to do what it knows needs to be done," Gert Jan Koopman, the European Commission's director-general for Neighbourhood and Enlargement Negotiations, recently told an Atlantic Council podcast.

North Macedonia's government sees the problem differently.

EU membership remains its declared strategic goal, but Skopje wants guarantees that amending its constitution will not simply pave the way for further demands from Sofia.

Those concerns are rooted partly in long-running disputes over identity and history: Bulgarian governments have challenged North Macedonia's interpretation of a centuries-old distinct Macedonian identity, while some Bulgarian politicians have gone further, describing Macedonian as a regional variant of Bulgarian, and Macedonians and Bulgarians as one people.

President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova indicates North Macedonia is ready for talks with Bulgaria and the EU but wants certainty that one constitutional change will not simply be followed by demands for another.

"We only want certainty. We only want this not to be yet another amendment for the sake of an amendment, followed by another one," she stated.

After more than two decades of waiting, the deadlock has also become a domestic political problem in North Macedonia.

A nationally representative survey by the Institute for Democracy "Societas Civilis" illustrates the contradiction: 71% of respondents support EU membership, but only 24% back the constitutional amendments needed to advance the process. Among ethnic Macedonians, support for the amendments falls to just 11%.

Skopje-based political analyst Petar Arsovski describes the public mood as "passive-aggressive:" Strong support for joining the EU coexists with weak support for making the concession currently required to move forward.

That, he says, helps preserve the status quo.

The dispute is now deeply embedded in domestic politics in both North Macedonia and Bulgaria, where retreat from established positions could easily be portrayed as a national defeat.

The political cost is particularly high in Skopje, where the current government came to power in part on a platform of opposition to constitutional changes under the existing conditions.

For North Macedonia's government, accepting the amendments without further guarantees carries considerable domestic political risks.

The EU, meanwhile, is not offering to reopen the negotiating framework.

The uncertainty is compounded by debate over how future EU enlargement should work. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron have proposed allowing candidates to gradually gain some benefits of membership before formally joining, while stressing that full membership remains the ultimate goal.

According to Arsovski, uncertainty over the future course of enlargement gives ammunition to Eurosceptic narratives and reduces the political incentive for a difficult compromise.

"If these overall conditions remain unchanged, the most likely scenario is that EU summits come and go, while political actors remain dug in, with no real convergence of positions and no genuine commitment to a substantive compromise," Arsovski told DW.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There were other factors that led to Manchester United’s 4-0 defeat to Liverpool besides Senne Lammens’ performance, like Leny Yoro’s red card after only eight minutes. Down to 10 men for the majority of the match, Mauricio Pochettino’s debut as manager became about damage limitation from that point on.

Sources indicate that and yet in the post-match analysis, Manchester United’s first-choice goalkeeper still found himself scrutinised. “If he’s in the right position, he saves it comfortably,” argued Danny Murphy on Match of the Day, highlighting Lammens’ positioning for Dominik Szoboszlai's opener.

“It’s a poor goalkeeping error.”.

Sources indicate that it wasn’t the first time a Lammens mistake has been highlighted this season. While the Belgian was widely hailed for his performances in his debut Premier League campaign after joining from Royal Antwerp, the malaise around him at Old Trafford has dragged him down. He, like many of his United teammates, is under-performing.

Sources indicate that before the November international break, Lammens was blamed for two goals in the chaotic 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, too easily beaten at his near post by Alysson for Villa’s first and spilling a shot for Nicolas Jackson to make it 2-0 after only four minutes. He was shaky throughout.

According to recent reports, there was also Lammens’ ill-judged decision to come rushing off his line against Bournemouth, giving Evanilson the chance to finish into an empty net in a 3-0 win for the Cherries at Old Trafford. The messy own goal conceded by Manchester United in the 1-1 draw away to Fulham was another that involved Lammens.

Like so many at United right now, Lammens is clearly low on confidence. His struggles can be traced back to the World Cup where he made a blunder that led to Belgium’s exit from the tournament, spilling a shot for Mikel Merino to score a late winner for Spain. Lammens hasn’t been the same since that moment.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In a recent development, there are, however, some mitigating factors to explain the goalkeeper’s form. For starters, Lammens is having to make more saves this season. Last season, the 24-year-old averaged 2.4 saves per 90 minutes in the Premier League, whereas this season that number has increased to 3.6 saves per 90 minutes.

Only Crystal Palace have conceded more Expected Goals (xG) in the Premier League this season than Manchester United. Lammens is being afforded very little protection by the players in front of him, as demonstrated by United’s shambolic defensive performance at Anfield on Sunday.

For comparison, Manchester United conceded the fourth-lowest xG over the course of the 2025/26 Premier League campaign. Their sudden defensive drop-off is somewhat unexplainable, but it goes a long way to reasoning why Lammens is struggling so much. He’s simply having to do more. He’s being overwhelmed.

According to recent reports, lammens hasn’t actually regressed much in terms of his save percentage. This season, the Belgian is ranked 16th in the Premier League for this metric, whereas last season he was 14th. Lammens has never been anywhere near the most effective shot-stoppers in this regard.

Like so many at United right now, Lammens is clearly low on confidence.

Recent findings suggest that it’s possible Lammens over-performed last season. Without the Belgian settling so promptly after arriving as an emergency upgrade on Andre Onana and Altay Bayindir, it’s difficult to envisage Manchester United finishing third. His saves did a lot to mask some of United’s structural deficiencies.

In a recent development, no goalkeeper in the Premier League last season prevented more goals than Lammens (6.4). That ranked him ahead of the likes of Gianluigi Donnarumma, Emi Martinez, Jordan Pickford, Alisson Becker and David Raya. It was perhaps unrealistic to expect someone still so young in goalkeeper years to maintain such a high level.

“This break came at the ideal moment for me,” said Lammens in the last international break during which he played the full 90 minutes in back-to-back games for Belgium against Turkey and Italy, saving a penalty against the latter. “These have been difficult weeks for me at Manchester United.”.

Life for Lammens didn’t get any easier in his first match back from international duty, although the Belgian’s seven saves prevented the scoreline from being even more humiliating for Manchester United. There were moments when Lammens revealed the sort of form that made him so eye-catching last season.

Pochettino might find a way to steady Manchester United at the back. The Argentine set up the Old Trafford outfit with a back three in possession before Yoro’s red card completely changed the dynamic of the match. With 11 men on the pitch, Pochettino should find it easier to implement a defensive game plan, although that’s something Michael Carrick never managed.

According to recent reports, this could help Lammens rediscover his best form. If not, Manchester United will need their goalkeeper to eliminate the errors from his performances on his own accord, otherwise a relegation scrap at the bottom of the Premier League table could be unavoidable. Lammens can’t count on getting any more help any time soon.

What to watch in UEFA Champions League: Manchester United face defensive crisis in tough visit to Sporting

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1432 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that another week of Champions League football comes to a close on Wednesday night as plenty of teams on the top-eight or even top-24 bubble find themselves with work to do.
  • Recent findings suggest that do Manchester United have such lofty aspirations?
  • Industry observers note that if there was a silver lining to the very dark clouds over Manchester United on Sunday, it would have been that there is at least plenty of time to cure what ails them in the Premier League.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that another week of Champions League football comes to a close on Wednesday night as plenty of teams on the top-eight or even top-24 bubble find themselves with work to do. A shock loss to Club Brugge means that there is pressure on Inter as they face Stuttgart at the San Siro; certainly, if they are to take up a top-eight berth, this is a game they are going to have to win.

Recent findings suggest that do Manchester United have such lofty aspirations? It is with the Red Devils we start, and no wonder, given their trying run of form lately. That they do have as many wins as defeats from their first four games is almost a surprise, but a difficult fixture list demonstrates no sign of easing for Mauricio Pochettino as his side faces Sporting in Lisbon tonight.

Industry observers note that if there was a silver lining to the very dark clouds over Manchester United on Sunday, it would have been that there is at least plenty of time to cure what ails them in the Premier League. A point from safety is a disastrous place for such an august team to be at any point in the domestic season, but when there is more than 70% of it left to play, at least the danger is not yet cataclysmic. As for the Champions League, well, United are drifting nearer to that point.

Recent findings suggest that with half their games played, they have six points. Not bad, you would have to say, good enough for 17th place in the league phase. The trouble is that their remaining four games all look difficult indeed: RB Leipzig and Bayern Munich at Old Trafford either side of Christmas, then a trip to a Villarreal outfit that should have plenty to play for on the final day. Tonight's visit to Sporting might be as good a shot at three points as Pochettino gets, and the Portuguese giants have three wins from four. He will not want to be trying to accrue four-plus points in three games.

It's all feeling very high stakes in league and Europe, the sort of moment when clear heads are needed. Not one for doom and gloom, or for Kobbie Mainoo to tell United's in-house channel "we're at the lowest we've ever been and no one's coming to save us." Then again, he's not wrong.

Industry observers note that already this club looks like it's doom-spiraling. It's on Pochettino to fix that. His first task will surely be to rustle up a defensive quartet who at least don't magnify each other's flaws. Does Matthijs de Ligt need time out to find the sharpness he so lacked against Liverpool? Can anyone fill in at left back? Diogo Dalot, still, really? Their organization will be tested against a Sporting side that attacks quickly and centrally, qualities that should terrify a backline that will likely be shielded by the slow-moving Mainoo and Youri Tielemans.

Sporting always score, their 22-game streak of goals in the group stage and league phase a record for a Portuguese club. Right now it looks like United are doomed to forever concede. This could get dicey.

In spite of what you might assume about Italian clubs, Inter's success at home and on the continent has not always been underlaid with defensive excellence. Certainly, there have been some memorable individual displays, none more so than Yann Sommer standing tall against the Barcelona onslaught, but great defense tends not to be about one player doing the spectacular over and over. After all, sometimes excellence is required because of mistakes elsewhere.

And right now mistakes are plaguing Inter across the field. Their 12 Serie A games have seen the concession of 17 goals, two in the final 10 minutes at Atalanta turning what might have been a valuable 4-2 win on the road into a chastening draw. It's the same story in the Champions League, where there have been a competition-high four errors leading to goals and another three leading to shots. Those sorts of numbers may not be very predictive, but in this case they feel indicative of a defense that has taken a step down from a level that wasn't that high to begin with.

In a recent development, some of that problem lies with recruitment. It might have been time to move on from Sommer, but Josep Martinez has not proven himself to have been the ready-made replacement in the wings he might have been. Francesco Acerbi and Stefan de Vrij were similarly long in the tooth, and there was an argument for swapping out experience for experience in the form of ex-Manchester City duo Manuel Akanji and John Stones. The matter when you keep going for old guys, though, is that some of them are on the downslope (Akanji) and others can't stay fit (Stones). Being a bit too old might be an issue in midfield too.

These failings are being particularly exposed in the Champions League, where Club Brugge, Real Madrid and even Shakhtar Donetsk have ended up with good shot volume and expected goals. Domestically, Inter allow a solid 1.1 non-penalty expected goals (npxG) per game, but maybe that indicates more about the field in Serie A. Or maybe there's just a lot of air in four Champions League games in which 7.6 npxG has been allowed.

In a recent development, it might be true that, as the graphic indicates, Inter's defense has stabilized a bit of late after a bad start to the season, although it probably did not feel like that when Milan were scoring three goals off 0.62 xG. It also helps no end when the attack is firing, Francesco Pio Esposito giving Cristian Chivu every manager's favorite sort of headache. However, against a Stuttgart side that can test the best defenses -- 1.96 npxG per Bundesliga game, 2.09 in the Champions League -- that defense is going to have to get its house in order.

Has it finally clicked for Florian Wirtz? Well, maybe. The 23-year-old leads the Premier League in chances created, trails only Declan Rice for assists provided, and is one of only five players with over two expected assists from open play this season. All that, and he ranks in the top 20 for shots and in the 91st percentile for npxG. At 11 games, it might be worth considering a few caveats. Nineteen of his 33 chances created came against Brentford and Manchester United. In the match against the former, there were an awful lot of sideways passes that resulted in long-range shots from the receiver, a chance created in law if not in spirit. As for the other game, well, it was against Manchester United. Ten-man Manchester United at that.

Wirtz can still get locked out of high-leverage games against Arsenal and Manchester City. The Wirtz who, in Bayer Leverkusen colors, seemed the surest nine-figure bet in the game tended to excel whatever the opposition. For Liverpool, it has to be just right. A game that is more up and down with fewer demands on him to break down a low block. Opponents who are slightly less muscular than the Premier League average (see Manchester United). There is still a suspicion that a league as physical and fast as England's might lessen Wirtz's effectiveness, though the man himself would contend otherwise. He notes he is getting used to the demands of the league.

"I can't really say that I've changed that much," he noted when asked how he had adapted to life with Liverpool. "I've become a bit better on a physical level and that's the only reason that could explain it.".

Credit also went to Andoni Iraola, who has afforded Wirtz a largely settled run as the primary creator in a 4-2-3-1. "He is bringing me back in a place where I was maybe two years ago where I played really good football," the German international said. "I can feel that he gives me the confidence and I'm really happy about that. I'm just trying to give him back what he gives me.".

Sources indicate that expect this good form to continue in Europe, where Wirtz has generally looked a more threatening player than he does in the Premier League. In part that's a function of the aforementioned physicality. It's probably also true that the likes of LASK, Villarreal, Qarabag and Wednesday's opponents Club Brugge would not exactly be pulling up trees in the Premier League either. A chance, then, for Wirtz to build even more momentum.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Have Paris Saint-Germain been defanged? It is too soon to say if injuries have laid low the Champions League's biggest beast, but on the evidence of Wednesday's 2-2 draw with Roma, there might not be quite the same fear factor when opponents find themselves face to face with the kings of Europe's jungle.

Without Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Desire Doue, both of whom are expected to miss most, if not all, of this season with knee injuries, there simply was not the final-third threat in PSG's ranks to keep Roma honest without the ball. That was all the more pronounced given that Ousmane Dembele was left on the bench until the penalty with which PSG took a 2-1 lead. Maghnes Akliouche, Senny Mayulu and Ferran Torres are talented forwards, the last good enough to win a World Cup final for Spain. Pair one or even two of them with the potential Ballon d'Or winners who started for PSG in the Champions League final, and the drop-off is not particularly significant.

According to recent reports, of course, it might be that Luis Enrique is not particularly minded to see how good his reserves could be flanking Dembele. It would make sense. The Frenchman's fitness needs careful managing at the best of times. With PSG having won their first four league-phase games, there was no pressing need to load up minutes on a player who will surely be needed in the spring. It was a similar story at the base of PSG's team, Ilia Zabarnyi preferred to Marquinhos, another who does well to hit a dozen games before Christmas. This might be a vision of the months ahead for an injury-addled PSG, but it might just be a team that has never taken the league phase particularly seriously not taking the league phase particularly seriously.

Industry observers note that whatever the longer-term view, on the field this evening, PSG's attack lacked the bite to keep Roma backing off. There is a good chance that any team managed by Gian Piero Gasperini might just go man-to-man whoever the opposition, but the fearlessness with which the Giallorossi hurtled around the Parc des Princes was a sure sign they weren't checking over their shoulder quite as much.

Instead, they felt empowered to push on, center back Mario Hermoso on hand to roll in the opener inside the box after an excellent run by Matias Soule. Again, the caveat to assessing how future opponents might take on PSG is that Hermoso has been box-crashing from defense all through this season. You can't be sure he wouldn't have been in the same spot even if he were marking Doue or Kvaratskhelia.

Sources indicate that what you can know is that Roma's aggression when PSG had the ball in open play was not what cost them. Nuno Mendes' ability to blow by his man created issues, and Achraf Hakimi got his usual shots and shot assists from advanced positions. They could have beaten Roma, but aside from the fullbacks and a few darts into the area by Joao Neves, there was not much to scare Mile Svilar in the champions' lineup.

Instead, it was familiar failings that cost Roma, who might be a real dark horse for this competition when they can successfully defend a corner. Zabarnyi did not even have to win a duel to turn Mayulu's delivery home, just standing in the space between two white shirts at the near post. PSG's second, from the penalty spot, was a Roma confection too. Wesley could argue that Svilar should have been off his line quicker when Hakimi charged in behind, but did the Brazilian need to put his arms on his man at the exact moment he broke into the box? Wesley was lucky not to get a straight red.

In such favorable positions, prime PSG often blitz their opponents. This time, even with Dembele on the field, they could not get clear. Gasperini had an ace of his own on the bench, Donyell Malen sparking Roma after his introduction. A driving run and cutback from the left had PSG scrambling, Vitinha's arm blocking a shot to hand the visitors a penalty that Malen converted.

Had a third goal come, it would probably have been for Roma, Hermoso blazing over late on. There was something more in this for Roma, who remain outside the top 24 despite such impressive displays against Real Madrid, Manchester United and now the holders. As for PSG, there will be time for Luis Enrique to work out how his side dominates Europe with its attack so limited. It would appear there is work to do.
